## What a standard invites. {#next}

::: {.road}
```{=html}
{{< include /sketches/roadmap.svg >}}
```
::: {.road-col .road-ink}
[Ships today]{.road-head}
[in datom 0.2.0]{.road-sub}

- **Versions:** nothing is overwritten
- **Hashes:** same values, same hash
- **Lineage:** parents and code, at exact versions
- **Sets:** pinned, citable releases
- **Access control:** per project, through the permissions your git host and storage already enforce
- **Open format:** parquet + JSON, readable from Python or any language
- **Runs on:** local folders or S3, with GitHub
:::

::: {.road-col .road-next .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
[Next]{.road-head}
[designed, not built yet]{.road-sub}

- **Python reader:** enough to serve an API
- **Access from lineage:** computed on top of today's permissions
- **datomanager:** governance across projects, including migration when storage has to move
- **Data products on datom:** a product layer, built for datom from the start
:::

::: {.road-col .road-open .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
[Open to anyone]{.road-head}
[no permission needed]{.road-sub}

- other languages
- other git hosts and storage backends
- EDC connectors
- data dictionaries in the metadata (an ALS file, say)
- data diffs between versions
- pipelines and dashboards on pinned versions
- [your idea]{.road-slot}
:::
:::

::: notes
"A standard isn't finished when it ships. It's finished when other people build on it."

1:00. Two clicks.

The left card is what ships in datom 0.2.0 today, ticked off. Say the access line out loud, because people will ask: access is controlled today, per project, by the permissions your git host and your storage already enforce. Writers need the repo; readers need read access to storage, and nothing else. There's no new auth system to run, and when someone leaves, removing their git and cloud access removes their datom access too.

The format is open: parquet and JSON, so Python, or anything else, can read the files today. A Python datom reader, one that understands versions and sets, is next.

Click: next, designed but not built. A Python reader, enough to serve an API. Access computed from lineage, on top of today's permissions: who can read a derived table follows from what it was derived from. datomanager, for governance across projects, and that includes managed migration when storage has to move. And data products on datom: a product layer designed for datom from the start. That's new work, not daapr moving over; daapr carries on as its own package.

Click: open to anyone. Nobody has claimed these: other languages, other git hosts and storage backends, EDC connectors, data dictionaries carried in the metadata (an ALS file, say), diffs between versions, and pipelines and dashboards that read pinned versions. The format is open, so none of them needs permission. The last slot is yours.
:::
